analysis.one_liner: Blocks FDA tobacco regulation while conditioning federal health grants on state youth-access rules.
analysis.headline: Introduced in 1997 with zero cosponsors, the bill died in a House subcommittee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill was titled a youth smoking prevention act, but its opening provision did something very different: it declared that the Secretary of Health and Human Services has no authority under existing federal law to regulate the manufacture, labeling, sale, or advertising of tobacco. In place of that regulation, it would condition federal preventive-health block grants on states adopting a list of youth-access rules, such as banning sales to people under 18, restricting vending machines, keeping billboards away from schools and playgrounds, and licensing cigarette retailers.
analysis.who_benefits: Tobacco manufacturers and advertisers benefit most if it passes: the bill removes the federal government's power to regulate how their products are made, labeled, and marketed, converting a direct regulatory threat into a state-by-state grant condition. Retailers also benefit from a uniform, state-administered system, and states gain federal enforcement funding.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that the Secretary of Health and Human Services has no authority under the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, the Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act, or the Smokeless Tobacco Act to regulate tobacco manufacture, labeling, sale, distribution, or advertising.

Federal authority over tobacco sale, distribution, and promotion would instead be enforced only as a condition on states receiving preventive-health block grants, with enforcement funded out of those grants.
The bill requires states to adopt youth-access laws, bans tobacco brand logos on items marketed to minors, and restricts tobacco billboards within sight of schools and playgrounds.

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the strongest available federal tool for regulating tobacco manufacturing and marketing would be off the table, so the main cost falls on public health in general. Teenagers would also face fines, community service, and mandatory education for buying cigarettes, and states that did not adopt the required laws would lose escalating shares of their health block grants, up to 80%.
analysis.who_pays_short: Public health, and teens facing fines

drawbacks.text: The bill would prohibit minors from purchasing tobacco, fining them up to $100 plus community service and education for repeat violations, punishing the young buyer rather than only the seller.

States that did not enact the required laws would lose 20% of their block grant at first and up to 80% for continued noncompliance, cutting substance-abuse prevention and treatment funding in those states.

The advertising restrictions are narrow: billboards only near schools and playgrounds, and a logo ban only on items marketed specifically to minors, leaving most tobacco advertising untouched once FDA authority is removed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The youth-access provisions are real but modest: age checks, vending machine rules, and billboard setbacks are the kind of measures states were already adopting, and they are enforced only through grant conditions. The price for them is permanent: the bill would strip the federal government of authority to regulate tobacco manufacturing, labeling, and advertising outright, which at the time was the strongest regulatory avenue available. Even taking the bill's stated goal seriously, the trade favors the industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee in February 1997, sent to its Health and Environment Subcommittee a week later, and then sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Scotty Baesler, a Democrat from tobacco-growing Kentucky, introduced the bill on February 4, 1997, with no cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce, which sent it to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment on February 10, 1997; no further action is recorded.
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill was never brought to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public was better off because the bill died: its core effect would have been to remove FDA authority over tobacco manufacturing and advertising, and the youth-access rules it offered in exchange were far weaker than that authority. Tobacco makers, meanwhile, gained nothing, since they were no worse off than before.

for.name: Rep. Scotty Baesler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; it carried no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Commerce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health and Environment Subcommittee on February 10, 1997, and took no further recorded action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had a single sponsor, so no partisan split can be measured; the sponsor was a Democrat from a major tobacco-growing state.

industries.note: The bill's central provision wipes out federal authority to regulate how cigarettes are manufactured, labeled, and advertised, replacing direct regulation with state grant conditions. It came at a moment when the government had just asserted that authority, so the bill would have protected the industry's core marketing freedom while its supporters could point to youth-access rules.

Retailers would take on licensing, employee-notice, and inspection duties, but enforcement is federally funded through block grants and the products themselves stay fully on sale. The heavier restrictions fall elsewhere.

Tobacco billboards would be barred within sight of schools and playgrounds, costing the outdoor ad industry some accounts. The loss is small and only exists if the bill's larger deregulation also passed.
Vending machines would be limited to supervised locations, bars, private clubs, or age-control-equipped machines, cutting into that sales channel.
